vignette:
The patient sits at the edge of the ranger station, binoculars resting on his knee, scanning the acacia-dotted horizon. He does this every morning before dawn-not because he expects poachers or wandering elephants, but because the wide, open landscape is the only place where his eyes can rest. He tells me this in the first session, his voice soft and deliberate, as if each word has to be carried across a great distance.

His name is Kofi. He is forty-seven, single, born in the eastern region of a country that was torn apart by civil war for nearly a decade. He was a schoolteacher then, living in a small town with his wife and two young daughters. The war came slowly at first-rumors, curfews, the distant thud of artillery. Then one afternoon, armed men entered the village. He remembers the smell of burning maize and the sound of a child screaming, but not his own voice when he tried to call out. He hid beneath the floorboards of his neighbor's house for nearly fourteen hours. When he emerged, his house was gone. His family was gone. He walked for three days through the bush, past bodies, past the hollowed shells of trucks, past the silence of a village that had once been full of life.

He crossed the border and eventually found work as a ranger in a large national park several hundred miles away. The job suits him in ways he did not anticipate-the solitude, the predictable rhythm of patrols, the constant need to watch what moves in the underbrush. But the park also triggers him. The crack of a dry branch under a baboon's foot sends his heart racing. The smell of woodsmoke from a nearby camp makes him dizzy with nausea. He avoids the northern sector of the reserve because an abandoned stone bridge there reminded him of the burned market in his hometown. He has not told his supervisor why he refuses to go that way; he simply says the trails are unsafe.

At night, he does not sleep in the staff quarters. Instead, he sleeps in the back of his patrol vehicle, a rusted Land Cruiser, with the doors locked and a machete under the seat. He tells me he does this because it feels safer-the metal walls, the ability to drive away. But even there, the dreams come. He sees his daughters running through a field of grass that turns to ash. He wakes up drenched, fists clenched, convinced he hears the sound of footsteps outside. He has not had a full night's rest in over two years.

The hypervigilance follows him everywhere. In the grocery store, he positions himself with his back to the wall. When a helicopter flies over the park, he drops to a crouch before he can think. He flinches when people approach him from behind. He has stopped attending the monthly ranger gatherings, because the noise of laughter and conversation feels like a thin skin stretched over something terrible. He feels disconnected from the other rangers, who joke about animals and complain about tourists. They do not know what he saw. He does not want them to know.

He has thought about leaving the park, moving to a city, but the open sky is the only thing that calms him-when it is quiet. He finds himself staring at the horizon for hours, waiting. Waiting for something he cannot name. He tells me he is not depressed, not exactly. Just hollow. Like the space inside a baobab tree that has been eaten out by termites. He still does his job. He marks poacher tracks, reports water levels. But the passion is gone. He feels like a ghost drifting through a landscape that used to feel like home.

The PCL-5 score of seventy-four gives a number to what he already knows: the war never really ended. It just changed shape. Now it lives in the sound of a breaking twig, in the smell of rain on dry earth, in the way his hands shake when he hears a baby cry at the village clinic. He has not cried himself in three years. He tells me he has no tears left-only that constant, waiting silence.
